newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks likely to rebound but gains limited.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks likely to rebound but gains limited.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to rebound on Wednesday in line with U.S. markets, which recovered overnight after a plunge on Monday, brokers said.
But gains are expected to be limited amid an absence of fresh incentives to encourage buying.
They said the market was waiting for the Bank of Japan's "tankan" survey of business sentiment, which will be released at 8.50 a.m. (2350 GMT Tuesday), for possible direction.
On Tuesday, the Nikkei 225 finished at 20,341.93, down 94.21 points or 0.46 percent. Its September futures fell 40 to 20,370.

"If the 'tankan' figures are within expectations it will be a neutral factor, but if the figures are bad investors may give up on the recovery of the economy, which would be bad for stocks," said Yasuo Ueki, Nikko Securities general manager.
Economists' forecasts had ranged from minus four to plus four.

"There are worries of course that the government will opt for a rate hike if the economy is really doing well, but at the moment relief that the economy is not as glum as everyone thought it was is eclipsing the worries," said Hisao Suzuki, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities.

Some brokers said credit-tightening fears were minimised by the diffusion index for small manufacturers, which improved only slightly in June to minus seven from minus eight in March, but is forecast to fall to minus eight again in September.
Brokers hoped the cheerier tankan figures would help the Nikkei average break out of the boxed range it has been stuck in.
"Trade was led mostly by dealers, but the chance is emerging that the Nikkei average could rise past 21,000," said Katsuhiko Kodama, general manager at Toyo Securities.

But Credit Lyonnais strategist Shinichi Ichikawa said the gains were unlikely to be huge, as there seem to be few items on the horizon that could provide further pleasant surprises on the economy and prod the benchmark higher.

"The economy is unlikely to keep improving. Worries still remain concerning a strong yen and also bad loans, and in the mid-term the Nikkei average will not surge but rise gradually, going through correction phases," Nomura's Matsuura said.

Brokers said a rebound in U.S. markets overnight following a sharp fall on Monday was also psychologically supportive for stocks in the morning session. The Dow rose about 154 points or 2.02 percent to 7,758.
Turnover was 238 million shares, against 170 million by midday on Tuesday. Winners beat losers 719 to 289 while 226 issues were unchanged.
